To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

increasing intellectual property rights in developing countries has a positive effect on the growth and income inequality of developing countries, but a negative effect on the welfare and income inequality of developed countries.

increasing intellectual property rights protection in developing countries has a positive impact on the global economy but it may also increase income inequality in both the developed and developing countries.
increasing developing countries’ IPR protection is likely to lead to higher growth but lower welfare for developing countries, while it leads to higher growth, welfare and inequality for the North.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of increasing the developing country’s intellectual property rights protection, and the implications for China’s accession to WTO and the effects of China rising innovative capability on the global economy.

the effects of intellectual property rights protection and innovative capability of developing countries on the global economy, and it is the first to study this issue in the framework of a dynamic general equilibrium model with wealth heterogenei ty and endogenous innovation.
the effects of international IPRs on growth, welfare, and income inequality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
increasing intellectual property rights protection is not necessarily beneficial to global growth, welfare and inequality.
the impact of China’s accession to WTO is ambiguous.
China’s accession to WTO has been beneficial to the world economy, but the distribution of the benefits and costs has not been even.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
increasing intellectual property rights protection in developing countries has ambiguous effects on growth, welfare, income inequality and global welfare.
the effects of China's accession to WTO on global income inequality is ambiguous and the effect on China's income inequality depends on the level of China’s innovative capability.
the North’s increasing intellectual property rights protection and China’s accession to WTO in 2000 are likely to benefit the North but not the South.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of intellectual property rights protection depend on the degree of wealth heterogeneity in the North and South.
increasing intellectual property rights protection in China has been a double-edged sword.
increasing developing countries’ IPR protection can be a double-edged sword.
